title: Tragedy, Patience and a Narrow Door
overview: Jesus refuses to blame victims of disaster, urges people to turn their lives around while there is still time, heals a woman on the Sabbath, and grieves over Jerusalem as he heads toward it.

parts.label: Do disasters mean guilt? (vv. 1-5)
parts.note: People told Jesus that Pilate, the Roman governor, had killed some Galilean pilgrims at their sacrifices, and Jesus added a recent tower collapse in Jerusalem that killed eighteen. He denies the victims were worse than anyone else, and instead calls everyone listening to change their ways.

parts.label: The fig tree with no fruit (vv. 6-9)
parts.note: An owner wants a barren tree cut down, but the gardener asks for one more year of care. It is usually read as a picture of God's patience with his people, with a warning that the time is not endless.

parts.label: A bent woman set free (vv. 10-17)
parts.note: The synagogue leader objected that healing was work and could wait for another day. Jesus points out that people untie their animals for water on the Sabbath, so surely this woman, a full member of God's people bound for eighteen years, should be untied too.

parts.label: Mustard seed and yeast (vv. 18-21)
parts.note: God's kingdom starts tiny and hidden, like a seed that becomes a tree or a little yeast in a huge batch of dough. The point is that something easy to overlook will grow and spread through everything.

parts.label: The narrow door (vv. 22-30)
parts.note: Asked whether only a few will be saved, Jesus gives no number but urges real effort before the door is shut, warning that having eaten with him or heard him teach is not enough. People from every direction will join the great feast, and some who expected to be first will be last.

parts.label: Herod and the lament for Jerusalem (vv. 31-35)
parts.note: Warned that Herod, ruler of Galilee, wants him dead, Jesus calls him a fox and says he will keep working on his way to Jerusalem, the city where prophets had been killed. He grieves over it like a hen longing to shelter her chicks, ending with words from Psalm 118 that crowds will later shout as he enters the city.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the repeated warning that people will 'perish' points mainly to the coming destruction of Jerusalem by Rome or mainly to each person's final judgment before God.
think: When something terrible happens to someone, why do you think people so often look for a reason they must have deserved it?
